facts.statement: Argentavis magnificens was described by Campbell and Tonni in 1980.
facts.quote: parent_authority: Campbell & Tonni 1980

facts.statement: The only known species of the genus Argentavis is A. magnificens.
facts.quote: species: magnificens

facts.statement: Argentavis lived during the Late Miocene epoch, specifically the Huayquerian age.
facts.quote: dating to the Late Miocene (Huayquerian)

facts.statement: Fossils of Argentavis have been found in central and northwestern Argentina.
facts.quote: in central and northwestern Argentina

facts.statement: Argentavis had a wingspan estimated at around 5 to 6 meters.
facts.quote: wingspan of around 5 - 6 m

facts.statement: Argentavis has the second-largest wingspan of any known flying bird, surpassed only by Pelagornis sandersi.
facts.quote: only surpassed by that of Pelagornis sandersi

facts.statement: Argentavis is the heaviest known flying bird, with a weight of up to 70 to 72 kilograms.
facts.quote: still remains the heaviest flying bird weighing up to 70 - 72 kg

facts.statement: The first remains of Argentavis were discovered by Rosendo Pascual and Eduardo Tonni.
facts.quote: by Rosendo Pascual and Eduardo Tonni

facts.statement: The holotype specimen was found at the Salinas Grandes de Hidalgo locality in the Cerro Azul Formation of La Pampa Province, Argentina.
facts.quote: at the Salinas Grandes de Hidalgo locality in the Huayquerian Epecuén (now Cerro Azul) Formation of La Pampa Province, Argentina

facts.statement: A cast of the holotype specimen is held at the Los Angeles County Museum.
facts.quote: It was cast at the Los Angeles County Museum

facts.statement: The name Argentavis is derived from Latin words for silver and bird, referencing the country of Argentina where it was found.
facts.quote: The generic name Argentavis comes from the Latin "argentum", meaning silver, and "avis", meaning bird, and was used in reference to Argentina

facts.statement: The specific name magnificens means magnificent in Latin.
facts.quote: The specific name magnificens comes from the same word in Latin, meaning magnificent

facts.statement: The original fossil material is housed at the Museo de La Plata under the catalog number MLP 65-VII-29-49.
facts.quote: The material was then brought to the Museo de La Plata and housed under specimen number MLP 65-VII-29-49

facts.statement: Kenneth Campbell Jr. described three additional specimens of Argentavis in a 1995 paper.
facts.quote: Campbell would go on to describe three additional specimens of Argentavis in a 1995 paper

facts.statement: One additional specimen was collected by Galilio Scaglia in March 1982 from the Cerro Azul Formation.
facts.quote: The specimen was collected from the genus' type horizon, the Cerro Azul Formation of Argentina, in March of 1982 by Galilio Scaglia

facts.statement: One of the additional specimens was found approximately 60 km west of the type locality near Carhué.
facts.quote: However, it was found roughly 60km west of the type locality at a site near Carhué

facts.statement: In 2012, Marcos Cenizo and colleagues re-evaluated a specimen and assigned it to the family Phorusrhacidae rather than Argentavis.
facts.quote: Marcos Cenizo and colleagues would revisit this element in 2012 and refer it to the family Phorusrhacidae instead

facts.statement: Two other specimens were found in the Andalhualá Formation, about 1200 km northwest of the type locality.
facts.quote: The other specimens were found in the Andalhualá Formation of the Valle de Santa María, approximately 1200 km northwest of Argentavis' type locality

facts.statement: Radioisotope dating of the Andalhualá Formation yielded ages of 6.02 and 6.68 million years ago.
facts.quote: Two radioisotope dates were given for this formation in a 1979 publication by Marshall and colleagues, giving dates of 6.02 and 6.68 mya

facts.statement: Argentavis is classified as a member of the family Teratornithidae.
facts.quote: Argentavis is a member of the family Teratornithidae

facts.statement: Among Teratornithidae, A. magnificens is the second-oldest species, older than all others except Taubatornis campbelli.
facts.quote: A. magnificens is the second-oldest of these taxa, surpassed only by Taubatornis campbelli

facts.statement: The holotype skeleton is severely fractured, though crushing is limited except for the skull parts.
facts.quote: The bones of the holotype of Argentavis are severely fractured, although crushing is minimal aside from the preserved skull elements

facts.statement: The preserved part of the ulna lacks any diagnostic features.
facts.quote: the preserved portion of the ulna having no diagnostic characters at all

facts.statement: A partial claw bone found later associated with the holotype has not yet been described.
facts.quote: the partial ungual phalange later discovered on the holotype lacks a description

facts.statement: The quadrate bone of Argentavis has a quadratojugal socket positioned farther back and a mandibular articulation surface that extends more anterioventrally compared to Teratornis.
facts.quote: The quadratojugal socket is positioned farther back, and the surface for mandibular articulation extends more anterioventrally, but not as far forwards proportionally.

facts.statement: The coracoid shaft of Argentavis is laterally compressed near the humerus and features an anterior-glenoid facet that is nearly flat.
facts.quote: The shaft of the coracoid is laterally compressed near the humerus, with the anterior-glenoid facet nearly flat.

facts.statement: When viewed from above, the humeral shaft of Argentavis appears sigmoid or S-shaped.
facts.quote: The humeral shaft also appears sigmoid (s-shaped) when looking at it from above.

facts.statement: The deltoid crest on the humerus of Argentavis features a pronounced knob, though the distal portion of this crest is not preserved in the fossil record.
facts.quote: The deltoid crest features a pronounced knob, although its distal portion is not preserved.

facts.statement: The tibiotarsus of Argentavis is slightly curved when viewed from the front and has an underdeveloped fibular crest, differing from Teratornis.
facts.quote: The tibiotarsus differs from that of Teratornis by being slightly curved when viewed from the front, although this might be due in part to breakage, and in having an underdeveloped fibular crest.

facts.statement: Campbell and Tonni initially estimated the wingspan of Argentavis to be between 6.5 and 7.5 meters in their 1980 description.
facts.quote: The initial description by Campbell and Tonni in 1980 tentatively estimated the wingspan of Argentavis between 6.5 to 7.5 m based on comparisons with Teratornis merriami.

facts.statement: A 1983 study estimated the wingspan of Argentavis as high as 8.3 meters by scaling dimensions from the California condor.
facts.quote: The 1983 study by the same authors estimated the wingspan of Argentavis by scaling up the dimensions of the California condor, with the highest estimate being 8.3 m and other estimates between 5.7 to 6.4 m.

facts.statement: Recent research in 2024 suggests that the 8.3-meter wingspan estimate for Argentavis is an outlier.
facts.quote: In their supplementary material of the 2024 paper, Gayford and colleagues considered the 8.3 m estimate to be an outlier.

facts.statement: A 2010 study estimated the wing skeleton length of Argentavis at 1.83 meters, suggesting it likely had a smaller wingspan than previously thought unless it possessed significantly longer primary feathers.
facts.quote: In 2010, Mayr and Rubilar-Rogers estimated the wing skeleton length of Argentavis and Pelagornis chilensis at 1.83 m and 2.1 m respectively, with P. chilensis having an estimated wingspan of 5.2 to 6.1 m, suggesting that Argentavis probably had a smaller wingspan unless it had much longer primary feathers.

facts.statement: Daniel Ksepka estimated the wingspan of Argentavis to be between 5.09 and 6.07 meters, which is smaller than the 6.06 to 7.38 meters estimated for Pelagornis sandersi.
facts.quote: In his 2014 description of Pelagornis sandersi, Daniel Ksepka estimated the wingspan of P. sandersi at 6.06 to 7.38 m, exceeding that of Argentavis which he estimated at 5.09 to 5.57 m and 5.70 to 6.07 m based on regression analyses and comparisons with the California condor respectively.

facts.statement: The wandering albatross, the living bird with the largest wingspan, reaches upwards of 3.5 meters, which is significantly smaller than estimates for Argentavis.
facts.quote: For comparison, the living bird with the largest wingspan is the wandering albatross, reaching upwards of 3.5 m.

facts.statement: Early estimates for the body mass of Argentavis ranged from 80 kg to 120 kg depending on the year of the study.
facts.quote: The initial description by Campbell and Tonni in 1980 tentatively estimated the body mass of Argentavis at 120 kg, while the 1983 paper by the same authors estimated its body mass at approximately 80 kg.

facts.statement: Later studies have refined the body mass estimate of Argentavis to between 70 and 72 kg.
facts.quote: Subsequent studies have suggested a lower body mass estimate between 70 and 72 kg.

facts.statement: Estimates for Argentavis suggest a wing area of 8.11 m² and a wing loading of approximately 8.64 kg/m².
facts.quote: A number of estimates related to wing loading have been produced for Argentavis, most notably the wing area, estimated at 8.11 m2, and the wing loading, estimated at 84.6 N/m2 (1.77 lb/ft2), or about 8.64 kg/m2.

facts.statement: Argentavis likely laid one or two eggs weighing about 1 kg every two years.
facts.quote: Paleobiology Life history Comparison with extant birds suggests Argentavis laid one or two eggs with a mass of around 1 kg every two years.

facts.statement: Due to its size and flight capability, adult Argentavis rarely faced predation, dying mostly from old age or disease.
facts.quote: Because of its large size and ability to fly, Argentavis suffered hardly any predation, and mortality was mainly related to old age and disease in adults.

facts.statement: Argentavis primarily flew by soaring and used flapping flight only for short durations.
facts.quote: From the size and structure of its wings, it is inferred that A. magnificens flew mainly by soaring, using flapping flight only during short periods.

facts.statement: Research on modern condors suggests Argentavis could fly effectively in normal conditions despite spending little time flapping.
facts.quote: Studies on condor flight indicate that Argentavis was fully capable of flight in normal conditions, as modern large soaring birds spend very little time flapping their wings regardless of environment.

facts.statement: Argentavis had strong legs for a running start but relied on wind and vertical distance to flap its long wings effectively, especially for takeoff.
facts.quote: Although its legs were strong enough to provide it with a running or jumping start, the wings were simply too long to flap effectively until the bird had gained some vertical distance, meaning that, especially for takeoff, Argentavis would have depended on the wind.

facts.statement: Argentavis likely used thermal currents to stay aloft, with a minimum flight speed estimated at 11 m/s or 40 km/h.
facts.quote: It is probable that it utilised thermal currents to stay aloft, and it has been estimated that the minimal velocity for A. magnificens is about 11 m/s or 40 km/h.

facts.statement: Argentavis territories likely covered over 500 km², and the birds may have flown north-south patterns to avoid adverse winds while searching for food.
facts.quote: Argentavis territories probably measured more than 500 km2, which the birds screened for food, possibly utilizing a north–south flying pattern to avoid being slowed by adverse winds.

facts.statement: Based on brain morphology inferred from endocast reconstruction, Torres Etchegorry & Degrange (2024) suggested Argentavis was a scavenger or kleptoparasite living in open, sparsely vegetated areas.
facts.quote: Torres Etchegorry & Degrange (2024) suggested that Argentavis was a scavenger or even a kleptoparasitic bird, living in open areas without much vegetation, based on its probable brain morphology inferred from endocast reconstruction.

facts.statement: Argentavis belongs to the family Teratornithidae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Teratornithidae

facts.statement: Argentavis lived from the Tortonian to the Zanclean stages, approximately 8 to 5 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Tortonian to Zanclean (8 to 5 million years ago)

facts.statement: The genus Argentavis was named by Campbell and Tonni in 1980.
facts.quote: PBDB name: Argentavis (genus), Campbell and Tonni 1980
